    Chapter 5

    Symmetric Encryption: One Shared Key

    🤔 An attacker who doesn’t know the key changes “$100” into “$900”, and the bank’s decryption raises no alarm at all. How is that even possible?

    • ⏱️ ~9 min
    • 📚 10 sections
    • 🎮 6 interactive
    • ⭐ 270 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    5.1The idea#

    Symmetric encryption uses one key for both locking and unlocking. Alice and Bob each hold a copy of the same key.

    Analogy: a lockbox with two identical keys. Alice puts a letter inside, locks it and mails the box. Bob opens it with his copy of the key. Anyone who intercepts the box sees only a locked box.

    Symmetric encryption is extremely fast. A modern laptop can encrypt several gigabytes per second. That's why it's used for almost all actual data: web pages, video calls, files, disk drives.

    ✔ section read

    5.2The big problem: how do you share the key?#

    If Alice and Bob have never met, how does Bob get a copy of the key? If Alice sends it over the internet, Eve copies it. If she encrypts it, she needs another key to do that, and so on forever.

    It also gets out of hand quickly. If every pair of people needs its own key:

    People Keys needed
    2 1
    10 45
    1,000 499,500
    1 billion ~500 quadrillion

    This key distribution problem puzzled people for thousands of years. Armies used couriers with locked briefcases. The solution, public-key cryptography, came in the 1970s (Chapters 9 and 10).

    💡 Key idea: In practice, we use public-key cryptography to agree on a key, then symmetric encryption to protect the actual data. Every HTTPS connection works this way. Symmetric crypto does the heavy lifting because it's roughly a thousand times faster.

    5.3Two families: stream ciphers and block ciphers#

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Stream vs. block ciphers

    👍 Situational
    Stream cipher

    Keystream ⊕ plaintext

    • No padding; any length
    • Fast, low latency, great in software
    • Key + nonce reuse = two-time pad
    • Malleable without a MAC
    Best for: ChaCha20 in TLS, WireGuard, Signal
    👍 Situational
    Block cipher

    Scrambles fixed 16-byte blocks

    • Very well studied (AES)
    • Hardware acceleration everywhere
    • Flexible via modes
    • Needs a mode of operation to be useful
    • Wrong mode (ECB) leaks patterns
    Best for: AES-GCM almost everywhere
    ✔ section read

    5.4Stream ciphers#

    A stream cipher turns a short key into a long, random-looking keystream, then XORs it with the message (remember XOR from Chapter 3). It's a practical version of the one-time pad: instead of a truly random pad as long as the message, you get a pseudo-random pad generated from a short key.

    Cipher Status Notes
    RC4 ❌ Broken Was everywhere (WEP Wi-Fi, early HTTPS). Statistical biases in its output. Banned from TLS in 2015.
    ChaCha20 ✅ Modern, recommended Designed by Daniel J. Bernstein. Uses only additions, rotations and XORs ("ARX"), so it's fast on any processor, including phones without special AES hardware. Used in TLS, WireGuard, SSH and Signal.

    ⚠️ Watch out: a stream cipher must never reuse the same key + nonce combination. Doing so produces the same keystream, which is exactly the two-time pad problem from Chapter 3.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Stream ciphers

    ❌ Avoid
    RC4

    Was everywhere in the 90s and 2000s

    • Tiny and fast
    • Easy to implement
    • Statistically biased output
    • Broke WEP; banned from TLS in 2015
    Best for: Nothing, anymore
    ✅ Use it
    ChaCha20

    ARX design by Daniel J. Bernstein

    • Fast on any CPU, even without AES hardware
    • Only add, rotate and XOR: naturally constant time
    • Huge security margin
    • Slower than AES where AES-NI exists
    • Still needs Poly1305 for integrity
    Best for: Phones, IoT, TLS, WireGuard, SSH
    ✔ section read

    5.5Block ciphers: DES, 3DES and AES#

    Cipher Year Key size Block size Status
    DES 1977 56 bits 64 bits ❌ Broken by brute force (1998, in 56 hours)
    3DES (Triple DES) 1998 112 bits effective 64 bits ❌ Retired. Slow, and the small block size enables attacks (Sweet32, 2016). NIST disallowed it after 2023.
    AES 2001 128, 192 or 256 bits 128 bits ✅ The world standard

    AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) was chosen through an open, public competition run by NIST from 1997 to 2000. Fifteen designs from around the world were submitted and attacked by cryptographers. The winner, Rijndael, was designed by two Belgian cryptographers, Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen. It's now used everywhere: HTTPS, Wi-Fi, disk encryption, messaging apps, banking and government secrets.

    How AES scrambles data (the intuition)

    AES takes 16 bytes and arranges them in a 4×4 grid. Then it repeats a "round" of four steps many times: 10 rounds for a 128-bit key, 12 for 192-bit, 14 for 256-bit.

    Think of a Rubik's cube. Each round twists the cube in a way that depends on your key. After a few rounds, every byte of the output depends on every byte of the input and every bit of the key. Change one input bit, and about half of all output bits flip.

    Claude Shannon called the two ingredients:

    • Confusion: the relationship between key and ciphertext is hopelessly complicated (SubBytes, AddRoundKey).
    • Diffusion: a change anywhere spreads everywhere (ShiftRows, MixColumns).

    Modern CPUs have special AES instructions (Intel/AMD "AES-NI," ARM "Cryptography Extensions"), so AES runs at gigabytes per second and resists certain timing attacks.

    🧮 Math corner: the "blending" in MixColumns and the S-box use arithmetic in a finite field called GF(2⁸). It's a number system with exactly 256 elements, one for each possible byte, where addition is XOR and multiplication follows special rules that wrap around. It guarantees every operation can be undone with the key.

    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Block ciphers

    ❌ Avoid
    DES

    1977, 56-bit key

    • Historic: decades of public cryptanalysis
    • Brute-forced in 56 hours (1998)
    • 64-bit blocks
    Best for: History class
    ❌ Avoid
    3DES

    DES three times, 112-bit effective

    • Backwards compatible with DES hardware
    • No practical key-recovery attack
    • Slow (3 passes)
    • 64-bit blocks → Sweet32
    • Disallowed by NIST after 2023
    Best for: Legacy payment systems being migrated
    ✅ Use it
    AES

    Rijndael, the 2001 world standard

    • Open competition winner, 25 years of scrutiny
    • Hardware instructions (AES-NI, ARMv8)
    • 128/192/256-bit keys
    • Table-based software can leak timing
    • Only as good as its mode
    Best for: Everything: HTTPS, Wi-Fi, disks, messaging
    ⚠️ Legacy
    Blowfish

    1993, up to 448-bit keys

    • Unbroken core design
    • Lives on inside bcrypt
    • 64-bit blocks (Sweet32)
    • Slow key setup
    Best for: Only inside bcrypt
    ✔ section read

    5.6Modes of operation: encrypting more than 16 bytes#

    AES on its own only encrypts a single 16-byte block. To encrypt a 5 MB photo, you need a mode of operation: a rule for chaining blocks together. The choice of mode matters as much as the choice of cipher.

    ECB (Electronic Codebook): ❌ never use it

    Each block is encrypted independently with the same key. Simple, and badly broken: identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks.

    The famous demonstration is the "ECB penguin": encrypt a picture of the Linux penguin with ECB mode and you can still see the penguin in the encrypted image, because areas of the same color become the same encrypted pattern.

    🧪 Try it yourself (Python): three identical blocks in ECB mode give three identical ciphertext blocks. CBC mode doesn't.

    Python
    import secrets
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import Cipher, algorithms, modes

key = secrets.token_bytes(16)
plaintext = b"YELLOW SUBMARINE" * 3          # three identical 16-byte blocks

enc = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.ECB()).encryptor()
ct = enc.update(plaintext) + enc.finalize()
for i in range(0, len(ct), 16):
    print(ct[i:i+16].hex())
# e649ef630d47b3db50a8229109e31403
# e649ef630d47b3db50a8229109e31403   ← identical! the pattern leaks
# e649ef630d47b3db50a8229109e31403

iv = secrets.token_bytes(16)
enc = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.CBC(iv)).encryptor()
ct = enc.update(plaintext) + enc.finalize()
for i in range(0, len(ct), 16):
    print(ct[i:i+16].hex())
# 3d414db5de5966e6f81095c5f2fd2a61
# 12548cb0d2eea1530164de8171b26578   ← all different
# cd44a639e22bb72c14f0f663e16a9b36

    (Your hex values will differ because the key is random. The pattern is what matters.)

    CBC (Cipher Block Chaining): legacy, OK with care

    Before encrypting each block, XOR it with the previous ciphertext block. The first block is XORed with a random IV. Now identical plaintext blocks look different.

    Downsides: encryption can't be parallelized, the message must be padded to a multiple of 16 bytes, and without a separate integrity check it's vulnerable to "padding oracle" attacks (Chapter 18).

    Padding (PKCS#7): if the last block needs N more bytes, add N bytes each with the value N.

    CTR (Counter): turn a block cipher into a stream cipher

    Encrypt a sequence of counter values (nonce‖1, nonce‖2, nonce‖3 …) to produce a keystream, then XOR it with the plaintext. Fast, parallel, no padding needed.

    ⚠️ The nonce must never repeat with the same key.

    GCM (Galois/Counter Mode): ✅ the modern default

    GCM = CTR mode for secrecy + a built-in authentication tag for integrity. It's an "AEAD" mode (section 5.8). AES-GCM protects most HTTPS traffic in the world.

    Mode comparison

    Mode Hides patterns? Detects tampering? Parallel? Needs padding? Verdict
    ECB ❌ No ❌ No ✅ Yes ❌ Never use
    CBC ✅ ❌ No Decrypt only Yes ⚠️ Legacy; only with a MAC
    CTR ✅ ❌ No ✅ No ⚠️ Only with a MAC
    GCM ✅ ✅ Yes ✅ No ✅ Use this
    XTS ✅ ❌ ✅ No ✅ For disk encryption only
    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Modes of operation

    ❌ Avoid
    ECB

    Each block alone

    • Simple, parallel
    • Identical blocks → identical ciphertext (the penguin!)
    • No integrity
    Best for: Never
    ⚠️ Legacy
    CBC

    Chain each block to the previous one

    • Hides patterns
    • Supported everywhere
    • Needs padding → padding oracles
    • Encryption not parallel
    • Needs a separate MAC
    Best for: Legacy systems, with Encrypt-then-MAC
    👍 Situational
    CTR

    Encrypt a counter → keystream

    • Parallel and seekable
    • No padding
    • Nonce reuse is fatal
    • Malleable: bits flip straight through
    Best for: Building block (inside GCM)
    ✅ Use it
    GCM

    CTR + authentication tag (AEAD)

    • Secrecy + integrity in one step
    • Fast with hardware
    • Protects most HTTPS traffic
    • Nonce reuse leaks data AND allows forgery
    • Rotate keys before ~2³² random nonces
    Best for: Default for new designs
    👍 Situational
    XTS

    Tweakable mode for disk sectors

    • Same-size output: fits disk sectors
    • Each sector encrypted differently
    • No integrity (by design)
    • Only for storage
    Best for: BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS
    ✔ section read

    5.7Encryption without integrity is dangerous#

    Here's a surprise for most people: an attacker can change encrypted data without knowing the key.

    With stream ciphers and CTR mode, flipping a bit in the ciphertext flips the same bit in the decrypted plaintext. If Mallory can guess what the message says (for example, a bank transfer with a known format), she can change it precisely.

    🧪 Try it yourself (Python): turn "$100" into "$900" without the key.

    Python
    import secrets
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import Cipher, algorithms, modes

key = secrets.token_bytes(16)
nonce = secrets.token_bytes(16)

# Alice encrypts a payment instruction
enc = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.CTR(nonce)).encryptor()
ct = bytearray(enc.update(b"PAY BOB $100") + enc.finalize())

# Mallory doesn't know the key, but guesses the format.
# Position 9 holds "1". She flips exactly the bits that turn "1" into "9".
ct[9] ^= ord("1") ^ ord("9")

# Bob decrypts the modified message
dec = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.CTR(nonce)).decryptor()
print(dec.update(bytes(ct)) + dec.finalize())   # b'PAY BOB $900'  ← no error!

    Bob's decryption succeeds with no warning. This property is called malleability, and it's why modern systems never use encryption without an integrity check.

    5.8AEAD: encryption and integrity in one step#

    AEAD stands for Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data. It's the modern, correct way to encrypt. It gives you:

    • Confidentiality: the data is secret.
    • Integrity and authenticity: any change to the ciphertext, nonce or associated data is detected.

    Associated data is information that must not be tampered with but doesn't need to be secret. Example: the header of a network packet says where it's going. Routers need to read it, so it can't be encrypted, but you want to detect if someone changes it.

    The two AEADs you'll see everywhere:

    AEAD Where it shines Used in
    AES-GCM (128 or 256) Computers with AES hardware TLS, IPsec, SSH, disk tools, cloud storage
    ChaCha20-Poly1305 Phones and devices without AES hardware; simple to implement safely TLS, WireGuard, SSH, Signal, Android

    ⚠️ Watch out: nonce reuse in AES-GCM is catastrophic. Reusing a nonce with the same key reveals the XOR of the two messages and lets the attacker forge new valid messages. Safe approaches:

    • Use a counter that never repeats (TLS does this), or
    • Use a random 96-bit nonce and rotate the key well before 2³² (about 4 billion) messages, or
    • Use XChaCha20-Poly1305 (192-bit nonce, so random nonces are safe), or AES-GCM-SIV, which is designed to survive accidental nonce reuse.

    🧪 Try it yourself (Python): AES-256-GCM with tamper detection.

    Python
    import secrets
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM

key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)   # 32 random bytes
aesgcm = AESGCM(key)

nonce = secrets.token_bytes(12)             # 96-bit nonce: unique per message!
header = b"to:bob"                          # associated data: visible but protected
ciphertext = aesgcm.encrypt(nonce, b"Meet me at 5pm", header)
print(ciphertext.hex())                     # 14 bytes of ciphertext + 16-byte tag = 30 bytes

print(aesgcm.decrypt(nonce, ciphertext, header))   # b'Meet me at 5pm'

# Mallory flips one bit...
tampered = bytearray(ciphertext)
tampered[0] ^= 0x01
try:
    aesgcm.decrypt(nonce, bytes(tampered), header)
except Exception as e:
    print("Tampering detected!", type(e).__name__)  # Tampering detected! InvalidTag

    And ChaCha20-Poly1305 works the same way:

    Python
    import secrets
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import ChaCha20Poly1305

key = ChaCha20Poly1305.generate_key()
chacha = ChaCha20Poly1305(key)
nonce = secrets.token_bytes(12)
ct = chacha.encrypt(nonce, b"hello from my phone", None)   # None = no associated data
print(chacha.decrypt(nonce, ct, None))                     # b'hello from my phone'
    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    AEADs: the modern way to encrypt

    ✅ Use it
    AES-GCM

    AES + Galois MAC

    • Blazing fast with AES-NI
    • Standard in TLS, IPsec, SSH, cloud
    • Catastrophic on nonce reuse
    • Slow and tricky in pure software
    Best for: Servers and laptops
    ✅ Use it
    ChaCha20-Poly1305

    Stream cipher + one-time MAC

    • Fast everywhere, even cheap phones
    • Simple to implement safely
    • Still needs unique nonces (96-bit)
    • Slightly slower than AES-NI on desktops
    Best for: Mobile, WireGuard, Signal
    ✅ Use it
    XChaCha20-Poly1305

    192-bit nonce variant

    • Random nonces are safe
    • Same speed as ChaCha20
    • Not in TLS
    • Fewer standard libraries
    Best for: Apps that pick random nonces
    ✅ Use it
    AES-GCM-SIV

    Nonce-misuse resistant

    • Survives accidental nonce reuse (only reveals duplicates)
    • AES-NI speed
    • Two passes over the data
    • Less widely deployed
    Best for: When nonce uniqueness can’t be guaranteed

    5.9Encrypting a file from the command line#

    🧪 Try it yourself (OpenSSL): encrypt a file with a password.

    Terminal
    echo "Meet me at the library at 5pm" > secret.txt

# Encrypt (AES-256 in CBC mode; the key is derived from the password with PBKDF2)
openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -iter 600000 -salt \
  -in secret.txt -out secret.enc -pass pass:correct-horse

# Look at the encrypted bytes
xxd secret.enc | head -3
# 00000000: 5361 6c74 6564 5f5f d7b4 c733 f5af 4a13  Salted__...3..J.
# 00000010: c2b6 2612 340a 6f06 156a d918 04e6 f4e3  ..&.4.o..j......
# ...

# Decrypt with the right password
openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -iter 600000 \
  -in secret.enc -pass pass:correct-horse
# Meet me at the library at 5pm

# Wrong password
openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -iter 600000 \
  -in secret.enc -pass pass:wrong
# bad decrypt

    What's in the file: the first 8 bytes are literally the text Salted__, the next 8 are the random salt, and the rest is ciphertext. OpenSSL uses the password and salt to derive the AES key (more on that in Chapter 8).

    ⚠️ Watch out: openssl enc doesn't support AEAD modes like GCM, so this file has no integrity protection. It's fine for learning. For real file encryption, use a tool designed for it, such as age or GnuPG (gpg --symmetric), which authenticate the data.

    (On a shared computer, also avoid putting a password directly on the command line, since other users can sometimes see running commands. Leave off -pass and OpenSSL will prompt for it.)

    5.10Symmetric encryption summary#

    Name Type Key sizes Status today Notes
    Caesar, Vigenère Classical tiny ❌ Toy History only
    DES Block 56 ❌ Broken Brute-forced in 1998
    3DES Block 112/168 ❌ Retired Slow; 64-bit blocks
    RC4 Stream 40–2048 ❌ Broken Biased output
    Blowfish Block up to 448 ⚠️ Legacy 64-bit blocks; lives on inside bcrypt
    AES-GCM Block + AEAD mode 128/256 ✅ Recommended Hardware-accelerated
    ChaCha20-Poly1305 Stream + AEAD 256 ✅ Recommended Fast everywhere
    XChaCha20-Poly1305 Stream + AEAD 256 ✅ Recommended Safe with random nonces
    AES-XTS Block, disk mode 256/512 ✅ For disks Used by BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS
